source.title: Public asked to have their say on proposed new renewable energy company
source.summary: The proposed plans aim to reduce the cost of energy in the long-term, but won't be able to set bills.
source.evidence_text:
People across the country are being asked to have their say on proposals for a new renewable energy company owned by the Welsh government.
It would "develop and own" wind and solar plants, and support local communities to take an ownership stake.
The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government hope it can reduce the cost of bills in the long term, but the company would not directly set energy prices.
The company would not "replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household electricity prices", it said in a consultation document.
It would also "help more organisations use locally generated energy" and try to attract investment into Welsh energy infrastructure.
Enterprise Minister Adam Price told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast the government wanted an energy system that was "clean, cheap and owned by us".
It does not set out to replace the organisations that provide energy direct to customers, with the government inviting people for views on how it should operate.
The proposed plans aim to reduce the cost of energy in the long-term, but won't be able to set bills.
The Welsh government already owns a renewable onshore wind and solar developer - Trydan Gwyrdd Cymru , external (TGC).
Ministers in Cardiff are proposing to bring TGC together with other existing Welsh energy schemes, such as Ynni Cymru, which aims to expand locally-owned renewables and the government's energy service.
The consultation looks at establishing a Welsh Energy Wealth Fund to allow energy projects "to support the most vulnerable in Wales as well as those living in areas where projects are being delivered".
It added that its purpose would be to "help Wales reduce energy costs over time by developing and owning renewable energy assets" and "supporting local and community ownership, investing in smart local energy systems".
He said the organisation was bringing the different elements together "to create a single company that, if you like, has the range of expertise and the sort of critical mass of resources and knowledge to make a real difference".
Price said Wales was "an energy giant at the Industrial Revolution with coal, but unfortunately we didn't see the benefit of that being derived largely by our own people".
He added: "We don't want to make the same mistake with the huge potential that Wales has in this new energy revolution with renewable energy."
The minister said many of the levers for energy are decided at a UK level, but added that energy produced by a public energy company could allow "lower energy prices" through agreements with local large energy users.
It also proposes that the company could take stakes in larger schemes - suggesting this could involve offshore wind, marine energy and nuclear.
The plans were criticised by the Welsh Conservatives and Reform.
Janet Finch-Saunders, Welsh Conservative energy spokesperson, said: "While thousands of well-paid manufacturing jobs are being lost, the Welsh government's answer is another state-owned company and yet more wind turbines and solar farms across the Welsh countryside.
"Wales needs cheap, reliable energy to keep factories open, businesses competitive and household bills down."
Jason O'Connell, shadow cabinet minister for economy and transport, said: "Welsh families are already paying some of the highest energy bills in the UK, yet Plaid wants to build a publicly owned energy company instead of focusing on getting bills down.

lesson.title: Welsh Government Seeks Input on New State-Owned Renewable Energy Entity
lesson.overview: The Welsh government is seeking public consultation on a new state-owned energy entity designed to develop renewable assets, aiming to reduce long-term energy costs and foster community ownership, though it will not directly control consumer bills.
lesson.topic: Welsh Renewable Energy Policy and Public Consultation
news_brief_sentences: The Welsh government is soliciting public input on a new state-owned renewable energy entity.
This initiative aims to mitigate energy costs over time by developing and owning renewable energy assets and supporting local and community ownership.
Furthermore, it would endeavor to attract investment into Welsh energy infrastructure and facilitate more organizations using locally generated energy.
Currently, ministers are proposing to integrate Trydan Gwyrdd Cymru (TGC), an existing onshore wind and solar developer, with other Welsh energy schemes like Ynni Cymru.
The consolidation seeks to create a single entity possessing the necessary expertise and critical mass of resources to effect significant change in the energy sector.
Despite its objective to reduce expenses, the consultation states that the company would not replace existing energy suppliers or directly determine household electricity prices.
Enterprise Minister Adam Price articulated a vision for Wales to have an energy system that is "clean, cheap and owned by us."

Price contrasted this modern ambition with Wales's historical position as an "energy giant" during the Industrial Revolution, lamenting that the benefits of coal were not primarily derived by its own populace.
He emphasized the imperative to avoid repeating such oversights with the immense potential presented by the contemporary renewable energy revolution.
While many energy policy levers are determined at a UK level, Price suggested a public energy company could facilitate lower prices through specific agreements with large local energy consumers.
The consultation also explores establishing a Welsh Energy Wealth Fund, intended to ensure energy project benefits reach vulnerable individuals and communities affected by project implementation.
Furthermore, the new entity might acquire stakes in substantial energy ventures, including offshore wind, marine energy, and nuclear power.
However, the proposals have faced scrutiny and criticism from political opponents such as the Welsh Conservatives and Reform parties.

Janet Finch-Saunders, Welsh Conservative energy spokesperson, challenged the government's focus, stating that another state-owned company and more turbines are not the answer amidst manufacturing job losses.
She asserted that Wales requires "cheap, reliable energy to keep factories open, businesses competitive and household bills down."

Jason O'Connell, Shadow Cabinet Minister, echoed similar concerns, questioning the priority of building a publicly owned energy entity over actively lowering current high energy bills for Welsh families.
